title: "Economic Satisfaction, Income and Wealth"

This report compares country-year summaries of satisfaction with the state of
the economy (ESS `stfeco`) with distributional series from the World Inequality
Database (WID). Country-year comparisons require observations of satisfaction,
income and wealth, and the validity rules below apply throughout the analysis.



## Data Validity

An observation is valid for comparison only when ESS flags the country-year as
reliable, both WID distributions contain all ten equal-split adult decile shares
and sum to one within 2.5 percentage points, and neither WID series marks the
year as extrapolated. The WID metadata does not identify all interpolated years.
Observations failing any rule are excluded from every section after
comparability.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Validity check                 | Passing country-years| Matched country-years|
|:------------------------------|---------------------:|---------------------:|
|Satisfaction estimate reliable |                   267|                   369|
|Complete valid wealth deciles  |                   369|                   369|
|Wealth not extrapolated        |                   369|                   369|
|Complete valid income deciles  |                   369|                   369|
|Income not extrapolated        |                   307|                   369|
|Pass all validity checks       |                   225|                   369|


:::
:::

## Satisfaction and Income/Wealth Association

The merged table uses the earliest matched observation in each two-year ESS
round and the corresponding WID distribution. It retains ESS reliability,
effective sample size, the selected post-tax income series where available,
and WID extrapolation flags. The full country-round table is available as
[data/processed/ess_wid_country_round.csv](data/processed/ess_wid_country_round.csv).

All summaries and correlations below use ESS observations flagged reliable.
Correlations are descriptive only; no significance tests are performed. Gini
values are approximated from WID's ten decile shares. Palma is the top 10% share
divided by the bottom 40% share; wealth Palma is missing when bottom-40 net wealth
is zero or negative.

Coefficients use finite pairs from reliable country-rounds; fewer than three

## Income and Wealth Distribution Change

This section summarizes annualized income and wealth distribution changes for
countries with matched economic satisfaction data. Years use two-year survey rounds
anchored at 2002; the earliest matched observation in each round is used. Each
reported transition compares consecutive selected survey observations, skipping
intervening distribution years. WID post-tax national-income shares are used where
available, with pre-tax shares as a fallback. For each transition, the score is
the mean absolute change across the nine cumulative decile-share cutoffs,
divided by the gap between survey observations. It is a magnitude in percentage
points per year; it does not indicate whether inequality rose or fell. The
metric uses the cumulative share profile directly, so it also applies when net
wealth shares are negative.

### Satisfaction Change Against Distribution Change

These transition-level comparisons relate the annualized absolute satisfaction mean
change to the annualized income or wealth distribution-change magnitude.
Same-interval comparisons match identical endpoint years. Lagged comparisons match both distribution endpoints 3 survey rounds earlier than the satisfaction endpoints; missing rounds are not skipped.
Only reliable satisfaction
transitions and non-extrapolated distribution transitions are included. Both measures
are magnitudes, so these associations do not show whether satisfaction or
inequality rose or fell. Correlations are descriptive.

## Economic Satisfaction Change

Satisfaction changes are calculated from the survey summaries. The mean measures
movement in average satisfaction with the state of the economy; the IQR measures
change in spread. Both are annualized absolute changes in satisfaction scale points.
Years use two-year survey rounds anchored at 2002, with the earliest available
valid matched observation in each round. Transitions compare consecutive selected
observations; gaps may span more than one round.

### Largest Satisfaction Mean and IQR Changes

The largest mean changes are ranked by annualized magnitude. The IQR panel shows
the observed IQR at both survey endpoints for the largest annualized IQR changes,
making the before/after spread visible. Segment color indicates whether the IQR
widened or narrowed; an asterisk marks an unreliable or unclassified endpoint.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figures/descriptive/distribution_change/ess/largest_changes.png){width=950}
:::
:::



## Middle-40% Wealth and Economic Satisfaction: Country Cases

This section focuses on the middle 40% of the wealth distribution (percentiles
50-90) and mean satisfaction with the state of the economy (`stfeco`, on a 0-10
scale). Wealth is measured as this group's **share of net personal wealth**, not
its absolute wealth. These are repeated country-level summaries, not observations
of the same individuals or evidence about middle-wealth respondents' satisfaction.

### Country Screening

To avoid comparisons directly involving the financial-crisis year, observations in
2008 are removed
before forming periods. This applies to both satisfaction and lagged wealth years.
Periods crossing an excluded year are split; each remaining complete sequence is assessed
if it meets the sample requirement. This does not remove possible crisis
aftereffects in subsequent years. Other report sections are unchanged.

For each country, all complete consecutive sequences of valid calendar-year observations
are screened. At least
3 exact one-year-lag pairs and
nonconstant measures in both comparisons are required. No missing years are filled
or bridged. We do not search arbitrary subwindows to maximize a coefficient.

Up to 5 positive and
5 negative cases are ranked by
same-year Pearson effect strength, with no fixed correlation cutoff. One period per
country and sign is retained; a country can appear in both groups when its association
changes direction between periods. Length breaks effect-strength ties rather than
determining which period is considered. Both comparisons use identical satisfaction years:
wealth at t versus satisfaction at t, and wealth at t-1 versus satisfaction at t.
The initial year supplies lagged wealth only. Only the selected cases appear below.

Available cases: **5 positive** and
**4 negative**. If fewer than five
qualified cases exist in either direction, the remaining places are left unfilled.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figures/middle_wealth_satisfaction/country_screening.png){width=800}
:::
:::


Bars show same-year Pearson correlations on the shared lag-supported sample.
"Strongest" means highest-ranked within the available cases, not necessarily a
large coefficient. Short series, time trends, outliers, and
selection on observed correlations can all produce apparently strong relationships;
these cases are exploratory and are not significance tests or causal estimates.

Persistence across the lag is informative as well as same-year effect strength.
Germany illustrates this: its 2009-2012 association is positive in both comparisons,
while its 2003-2006 association is negative in both. These are consistent directions
within each period, not one constant direction across Germany's full series.
Pearson/Spearman agreement and the lag interpretation below help distinguish persistent
patterns from associations that weaken or reverse. Three-pair cases remain fragile:
a large coefficient alone does not establish a robust or causal effect.

### Selected Cases

The table and scatterplot compare the shared eligible years within each selected period: teal
circles pair wealth and satisfaction in the same year; orange triangles pair wealth
in year t-1 with satisfaction in year t. Its solid and dashed fits and displayed
coefficients correspond to those two pairings. A negative Pearson r means higher
wealth share tends to coincide with lower satisfaction; it does not mean wealth
caused satisfaction to fall. Values near zero show little linear co-movement, while
values nearer -1 or +1 indicate stronger negative or positive co-movement. Pair
counts matter: series without sufficient exact one-year pairs are excluded entirely.

For the selected periods below, the accompanying interpretation instead compares the
two observed endpoints directly. Wealth movement is reported in **percentage points
of wealth share** and satisfaction movement in **scale points**. Opposite signs mean
the measures moved in opposite directions over that interval; matching signs mean
they moved in the same direction. This is a description of concurrent country-level
movement, not a causal effect or an individual-level relationship.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}

### Belgium: 2009-2012

Strongest negative association. 4 valid annual observations from 2009 to 2012.

Same-year Pearson r = -0.95; one-year-lag Pearson r = -0.66, using 3 paired years. From 2009 to 2012, the middle-40% wealth share increased by 1.34 percentage points, while mean economic satisfaction increased by 0.73 scale points.

Same-year Pearson -0.95; lagged Pearson -0.66. The association retains its direction but is weaker with the one-year lag. Only 3 paired years: exploratory. 

Spearman: same-year -1.00; one-year lag -0.50.
